header: Date: 2026-03-04 | Time: 15:16 PST | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Rossi (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Orion Head of ML), Liam Rodriguez (Orion Platform), Priya Nair (Orion CTO)
summary: POC scoping focused on cost modelling/unit economics for Orion's customer-support summarization workload. Discussed traffic shape, average/99th token lengths, target latency and p95/p99 SLOs, batching and KV/prefix caching opportunities, hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, and next steps to run benchmarks and produce a detailed per-token cost model.
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — we got Maya, Liam, Priya, and Elena on our side. Hi priya, hi maya.
[00:12] Maya: Hi Samir, hi Elena. Sorry for the slight delay on our side.
[00:17] Elena: No worries. I'll jump into the technical bits when we get to workload sizing.
[00:25] Samir: Cool. Goal for today is to scope the POC around cost modeling and unit economics — essentially can we estimate per-token costs, where batching and caching help, and what's realistic to hit in terms of latency and budget.
[00:38] Priya: Yes — our exec asks are: can we predict monthly cost if we route production traffic to Redwood, and what are the tradeoffs for hosted vs dedicated. Also important: can we keep p95 latency under 700ms for the chat summarization path.
[00:52] Samir: Good, that gives a target. Real quick, Maya, can you summarize the workload? Tokens per request, percent of long requests, embeddings?
[01:05] Maya: Sure. It's primarily summarization of multi-turn support conversations. Average request input is 350 tokens, average generated summary ~80 tokens. 10% of requests are long—over 2000 tokens (we trim some), and we also run embeddings for search on about 30% of sessions. Peak qps today is roughly 12 req/s across our EU+US clusters, with typical steady of 3-4 req/s.
[01:32] Elena: Good to know. For cost modeling we need two distributions: tokens per request (input + output) and concurrency profile. Also whether you have prefix caching opportunities — are many conversations repeats or identical preambles?
[01:44] Maya: There is a lot of repeated system prompt and user metadata, so prefix/KV caching seems promising. We estimate maybe 40% cache hit for the first part of the prompt.
[01:55] Samir: Perfect — that materially reduces token compute. Quick check: any compliance constraints — VPC, data residency, encryption?
[02:03] Priya: We need SOC2, SSO, and VPC peering for private deployment. For POC we can start hosted but need to exercise VPC connectivity for final test.
[02:15] Samir: That aligns with our flow: start hosted to iterate fast, then run the benchmark in your VPC or Dedicated environment to validate latency & throughput.
[02:25] Liam: On budget side, what's the baseline per-token cost we should expect? I've seen wide numbers online.
[02:33] Elena: Right — rough hosted numbers depend on model family, batch sizes, and quantization. For a ~7B-ish open model on GPU with good batching, you might see $0.0006–0.0012 per 1k tokens compute cost depending on utilization; larger models push that higher. But Redwood does batching/caching that can cut effective per-token by 20–60% depending on hit rate and batching. These are engineering estimates and we'll produce a spreadsheet with assumptions.
[03:05] Priya: Can you give an example calculation for our workload?
[03:10] Samir: Sure. If avg tokens per request (in+out) = 430, at 4 req/s steady = ~1720 tokens/s = ~148M tokens/day. If compute cost is $0.001 per 1k tokens, that's $148/day or ~$4.4k/month, but with cache hits at 40% and batching improvements we might get to $1.8–2.5k/month. Those are guesstimates; real numbers will depend on our benchmark.
[03:42] Maya: Ok that's in the ballpark. What about latency impacts when you batch? If we batch aggressively to save cost, do we blow past the 700ms p95?
[03:52] Elena: Good question. Batching increases effective throughput but adds queuing latency. We tune batching so latency SLOs aren't violated; two knobs: max batch size and batch latency window. For your steady qps, moderate batching (batch window 10–20ms, max size 8–16) typically yields cost wins without shifting p95 over our target. For tails (long requests) we use async routes or dedicated capacity to avoid queuing.
[04:19] Liam: What about KV/prefix caching we mentioned? How is that accounted for in the model?
[04:26] Elena: We model two components: 1) cached tokens (cost near zero to serve from kv cache, small overhead) and 2) uncached tokens billed at compute rate. So effective per-request compute_tokens = total_tokens * (1 - cache_hit_rate). With your 40% hit, a 430-token request becomes ~258 compute tokens. That halves cost roughly. Also we can cache KV at sequence level so generation cost can reduce too if summaries reuse templates.
[04:52] Priya: Are there fixed costs or minimums for Dedicated? We're thinking long-term maybe dedicated GPUs for predictable throughput.
[04:58] Samir: Dedicated has committed monthly pricing plus lower per-token compute rates because of reserved capacity. Example: a small dedicated pool might be $Xk/month with a capacity equivalent to Y tokens/s; the unit compute price drops significantly if you commit. We'll include committed vs pay-as-you-go scenarios in the spreadsheet. For a POC we can simulate dedicated unit economics with modeled discounts.
[05:22] Maya: For the benchmark run — what inputs do you need from us?
[05:26] Elena: We'll need the anonymized request logs (tokens per request), a set of representative prompts, a sample of long conversations, and spike scenarios. Also any proxy/networking constraints and the region preference. We'll provide scripts to replay traffic at controlled qps so we can measure p50/p95/p99 latency and token throughput.
[05:44] Maya: We can provide that. We'll scrub PII before sending.
[05:48] Samir: Great. On evaluation criteria — define success for the POC?
[05:52] Priya: Success is twofold: 1) demonstrated monthly cost forecast within 15% of actual measured during benchmark, and 2) confirm latency SLO p95 < 700ms on the production-like workload. If dedicated, also confirm scaling and failover.
[06:10] Elena: We'll also run quality checks — ensure generated summaries meet your internal metrics (ROUGE/precision) to ensure any quantization or smaller-model cost wins don't degrade quality beyond your threshold. We can add a small eval harness.
[06:23] Liam: How long for the POC timeline?
[06:26] Samir: Typical POC: 4–6 weeks. Week 1: data ingestion + align success criteria; Week 2: run hosted benchmarks; Week 3: tune batching/caching/quantization; Week 4: run final benchmark and produce cost model; optional Weeks 5–6 for dedicated verification and integration. We'll propose exact schedule after we see your availability.
[06:44] Maya: That fits. Any particular model families you recommend for our use case?
[06:49] Elena: For summarization you can choose between a mid-sized decoder-only 7B–13B optimized for latency vs a larger 30B for quality. Often we recommend starting with a 13B quantized variant if quality is important; cost differences show up clearly in the spreadsheet. We'll include comparative benchmarks.
[07:07] Priya: About quantization — does Redwood support 4-bit/8-bit mixed quant? Any caveats?
[07:12] Elena: Yes, we support quantized variants; it reduces GPU memory and can speed throughput but may slightly affect quality. We include quantization in the model comparatives and measure quality regressions against your eval set. For extreme tail latency we sometimes prefer CPU-offload or larger GPUs to reduce p99.
[07:30] Samir: Quick callouts — networking: if you want VPC for final verification we'll need to schedule a network test; also for SOC2 we'll share security docs.
[07:40] Priya: Please share SOC2 and encryption details.
[07:43] Samir: Will do. We'll attach links in the follow-up email.
[07:47] Maya: Anything else on cost knobs? Caching TTLs, eviction policies?
[07:52] Elena: TTLs matter. Short TTLs for session-level cache, longer TTLs for stable system prompts. Eviction policy is LRU by default. We can model several hit-rate scenarios (conservative, expected, optimistic) in the spreadsheet so you can see sensitivity.
[08:07] Liam: For embeddings — you mentioned they're 30% of sessions. Are we modeling them separately?
[08:12] Elena: Yes, embeddings are billed per-embedding unit and have different compute characteristics. We'll separate summarization token cost from embedding cost in the model and roll them up into a single monthly cost.
[08:23] Priya: If we decide dedicated, what's typical capacity sizing? We have peak 12 qps now — any rule of thumb?
[08:30] Elena: Depends on model and sequence length. As a rough thumb, a single A100-class GPU serving a quantized 13B model with batching can handle ~20–30 req/s at your avg token sizes with p95 under your target. But long requests change the calculus and may reduce concurrency; we size for 99th-percentile tokens. We'll include a recommended GPU pool and expected headroom.
[08:54] Samir: We'll capture that as an option in the cost model: pay-as-you-go hosted per-token vs reserved dedicated with monthly amortized GPU cost.
[09:03] Maya: Ok — timeline for you to send the cost spreadsheet?
[09:06] Samir: I'll send a first-pass today or tomorrow, final detailed version by Friday (2026-03-06).
[09:11] Elena: I'll prepare the replay scripts and benchmark deck and share by Tuesday (2026-03-10).
[09:18] Maya: We'll aim to get sample logs to you by Sunday (2026-03-08).
[09:23] Priya: Good. One last question: any hidden fees like logging/storage for KV cache?
[09:29] Samir: We'll call out storage costs for persisted cache and observability retention as separate line items in the spreadsheet — typically small relative to compute but visible.
[09:38] Liam: Sounds good.
[09:40] Samir: Great — recap of next steps: Samir send spreadsheet, Elena send benchmark plan and scripts, Maya send data samples, Liam confirm VPC/network details. We'll reconvene after the initial benchmark run.
[09:54] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[09:56] Maya: Thanks.
[09:58] Elena: Thanks, bye.
[10:00] Samir: Bye.
